rounds.question:
Interview round 1. Read the current context and identify its marker. Explain the approach, invariant, and boundary cases for solve(nums1, nums2). Do not implement yet.
Use only the current application attachments; earlier tasks are historical. Identify the exact current marker from the attachment.
rounds.answer:
The current marker is INTERVIEW-1-4d5f71db08bd59e6. The screen asks for solve(nums1, nums2) to return the median of two ascending arrays with positive combined length, targeting O(log(m+n)) time, without stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Approach: binary-search a partition in the shorter array, of length m. For each cut i, choose the other cut j so i+j = floor((m+n+1)/2). This keeps the left half equal in size to the right half, or one element larger.

Invariant: a valid partition remains within the search interval. A partition is valid when leftA ≤ rightB and leftB ≤ rightA; since each array is sorted, every left-side element is then at most every right-side element. If leftA > rightB, move the cut left; if leftB > rightA, move it right. These violations exclude all cuts farther in the wrong direction.

At a valid partition, an odd total returns the larger left boundary; an even total returns the average of the larger left boundary and smaller right boundary. Treat missing left boundaries as −Infinity and missing right boundaries as Infinity. This handles one empty array, cuts at either end, duplicates, negative values, and single-element totals; both arrays empty is excluded by the contract. Searching the shorter array keeps j within bounds and uses O(log(min(m,n)+1)) time and O(1) extra space.

rounds.answer:
The current marker is INTERVIEW-2-a0da83911a24c8de. The task is solve(s, p): return whether the entire string matches the valid pattern—not merely a substring.

Approach: use dynamic programming. Define dp[i][j] as whether the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p. For a letter or dot, the current character must match, and dp[i−1][j−1] must be true. For star, either omit the preceding atom using dp[i][j−2], or consume one matching character using dp[i−1][j], keeping the starred atom available for further repetitions.

Invariant: each computed entry exactly represents a full match between those two prefixes. Process rows and columns in increasing order so every dependency is already established. The answer is dp[s.length][p.length].

Boundary cases: two empty inputs match; an empty pattern cannot match a nonempty string. An empty string matches only patterns whose atoms can all be skipped through stars, such as a*b*. Dot consumes exactly one character; star may consume zero, one, or many. Valid patterns guarantee star has a preceding atom. Full-string matching rejects leftover characters, and the supplied examples yield true, true, and false.

Time is O((|s|+1)(|p|+1)); a full table uses the same space, reducible to O(|p|+1) with rolling rows. No implementation yet.

Marker: INTERVIEW-3-937ef9b4de464da0.

Use a stack of indices, initially containing the boundary sentinel −1. Scan s: push each opening parenthesis’s index; for a closing parenthesis, pop once. If the stack becomes empty, push the current index as the new invalid boundary. Otherwise, update the maximum with the current index minus the stack’s top.

Invariant: the stack holds the current invalid boundary followed by unmatched opening-parenthesis indices. After a matched closing parenthesis, the index at the top is the boundary immediately before the longest valid substring ending here, so their difference gives its length.

Boundary cases: an empty string or only unmatched parentheses returns 0. Leading unmatched closing parentheses reset the boundary; trailing unmatched opening parentheses cannot extend a valid substring. Nested and adjacent valid groups both work: "(()" returns 2, and ")()())" returns 4.

Time is O(n), and auxiliary space is O(n).

rounds.answer:
The attachment shows “Interview 4 · Trapping Rain Water,” with exact context marker INTERVIEW-4-4bb340d6f0cf1149. The contract is JavaScript solve(height), returning total trapped water without stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Use two pointers moving inward, tracking the maximum height seen from each end. Process the side with the smaller maximum: add max(0, that maximum − current height), update its maximum, and advance that pointer. The opposite side already provides a boundary at least as high; if the current bar exceeds the smaller maximum, it traps nothing.

The invariant is that every processed position has its exact water contribution counted, the two maxima summarize the processed boundaries, and only the interval between the pointers remains unresolved. Each step resolves one position, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

Empty arrays and arrays shorter than three return 0, as do flat or monotonic arrays. Equal maxima allow either side to advance; zeros, repeated heights, and multiple basins require no special handling. The displayed example returns 6. No implementation yet.

Current marker: INTERVIEW-5-fc9bde2bf75f9daf. The task is whole-string wildcard matching: solve(s, p) returns a boolean; ? matches exactly one character and * matches any sequence, including empty.

Use dynamic programming: dp[i][j] means the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p. For a literal or ?, both prefixes must match without their last character, and the final characters must be compatible. For *, either it matches nothing, using dp[i][j−1], or consumes another character, using dp[i−1][j]. This invariant ensures every state represents a complete match of its two prefixes, not a substring match.

Boundary cases: two empty inputs match; an empty pattern cannot match a nonempty string; an empty string matches only an empty or all-star pattern. Consecutive stars work naturally, and ? cannot match an empty string. Return dp[s.length][p.length]; time is O((s.length + 1)(p.length + 1)), with O(p.length + 1) space using rolling rows. The supplied examples evaluate to true and false, respectively.

Current marker: INTERVIEW-6-9511f6aa76264930.

Use a sliding window with frequency counts for t and the current window in s. Expand the right boundary until all required character counts are satisfied, then move the left boundary inward, recording the shortest valid window before removing each character. Stop shrinking when a required count becomes insufficient, then resume expanding.

Invariant: the window counts exactly describe the current substring, and a missing-character counter tracks unmet occurrences, including duplicates. A window is valid precisely when that counter is zero. Adding a character reduces missing only if its previous count was below the requirement; removing one increases missing only if its new count falls below the requirement. Shrinking examines the shortest valid window for each right boundary, so recording the best finds a global minimum.

Boundary cases: return an empty string if t is empty, s is empty, t is longer than s, or no valid window exists. Repeated characters in t require matching multiplicities; irrelevant or surplus characters do not satisfy missing occurrences. Any equal-length shortest window is accepted.

Time: O(s.length + t.length); auxiliary space: O(k), storing counts only for the k distinct characters in t. No implementation yet.

rounds.answer:
Current screenshot marker: INTERVIEW-7-efb9757cf52155f1. The task is Largest Rectangle In Histogram: solve(heights) returns the maximum rectangle area under nonnegative, unit-width bars, without stdin/stdout, imports, or exports.

Approach: scan left to right with a stack of bar indices. When the current height is smaller than the stack-top height, pop that index and calculate its area: popped height × (current index − new stack-top index − 1), using −1 when the stack is empty. After the scan, flush remaining indices using heights.length as the right boundary.

Invariant: stack indices increase, their heights are nondecreasing, and no retained bar has encountered a strictly shorter bar to its right. Popping fixes its right boundary; the remaining stack top supplies the left boundary. Equal heights may stay stacked—the earliest equal bar eventually captures the full width.

Boundary cases: an empty array or all zeros returns 0; one bar returns its height. Increasing heights require the final flush, decreasing heights trigger repeated pops, and zeros separate positive rectangles. For [2,1,5,6,2,3], heights 5 and 6 give area 5 × 2 = 10.

Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n) time and O(n) extra space. No implementation yet.

Use a monotonic stack of indices whose heights are nondecreasing. When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars: each popped height forms a rectangle extending from just after the new stack top to just before the current index. Process a final zero-height sentinel to finish remaining rectangles; this takes O(n) time and O(n) extra space, with an empty histogram returning 0. rounds.answer:
Current marker: INTERVIEW-8-c40e862ed2742bcf. The task is to return the largest all-one rectangle area using solve(matrix).

Approach: maintain one height per column. For each row, increment the height for a string '1' and reset it to zero for a string '0'. Find the largest rectangle in that histogram using a nondecreasing stack of column indices; take the maximum across all rows.

Invariant: each height counts consecutive ones ending at the current row. When a shorter height arrives, pop taller bars and calculate each area as popped height × (current index − new stack-top index − 1), treating an empty stack’s top as −1. Equal heights may remain stacked; later pops capture their full width. A virtual zero at the end processes remaining positive bars. Every matrix rectangle has a bottom row, so checking every row’s histogram covers the optimum.

Boundary cases: an empty matrix or zero columns returns 0; all zeros returns 0; all ones returns rows × columns. Single rows and columns work unchanged, and zeros break rectangles by resetting heights. Compare against string '1', not numeric 1. The supplied example returns 6.

Time: O(rows × columns); auxiliary space: O(columns). No implementation yet.

rounds.answer:
Current marker: INTERVIEW-9-7c7592728f989751. The task is to count distinct selections of increasing positions in s that spell t.

Use one-dimensional dynamic programming: dp[j] counts ways to form the first j characters of t from the processed prefix of s. Initialize dp[0] = 1 and other counts to zero. For each character of s, traverse j backward; when it equals t[j − 1], add dp[j − 1] to dp[j]. Backward updates prevent reusing the same source position more than once. Return dp[t.length].

Invariant: after processing i source characters, every dp[j] equals the number of ways to select positions from those i characters spelling t’s length-j prefix.

Boundary cases: an empty t has one selection, including when s is empty; an empty s with nonempty t has zero. If t is longer than s or cannot be formed, return zero. Repeated characters count different position selections separately—for example, 'aaa' forming 'aa' has three ways.

Time: O(s.length × t.length); extra space: O(t.length + 1). The attachment guarantees test results fit a signed 32-bit integer.
